content.summary: Welcome to Unit 11! In this reading module, you will explore how journalists report news stories, how people retell what others said using reported speech, and how verbs take objects followed by infinitives. You will read a fascinating text about famous media pranks and learn how to identify main ideas and specific details in news articles.

rules: When shifting from direct speech to reported speech, present simple changes to past simple.
Use 'say' without a direct object pronoun, but use 'tell' with an object pronoun like me, him, or us.
Verbs such as ask, want, tell, and persuade are followed by an object and an infinitive with 'to'.

commonTrap.explanation: Students often forget to change the tense when writing reported speech, or they mix up 'say' and 'tell'.

commonTrap.correct: He told me that he was tired, or he said that he was tired.

content.passageTitle: The Greatest April Fools in Television History
paragraphs: April first is a favorite day for journalists around the world. On this day, newspapers and television stations love to play a joke on the public. One of the most famous media hoaxes happened in nineteen fifty-seven. A respected BBC television program broadcast a special report about Swiss farmers who were enjoying an amazing spaghetti crop. The television cameras showed people pulling long strands of spaghetti from trees. Thousands of viewers watched the broadcast and believed every word.

After the show finished, many people called the television station because they wanted to know how to grow their own spaghetti trees in their gardens. The BBC told callers to place a piece of spaghetti in a tin of tomato sauce and hope for the best. Later, the broadcaster admitted they had made up the whole story. Although some critics thought it was silly, most people agreed that the hilarious prank was a masterpiece of broadcasting history.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Reporting the News with Passive Voice

content.summary: Practical guide on using the passive voice in present and past simple tenses for news reporting, reports, and formal writing in English.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Present Simple Passive Formula
blueprintItems.formula: Object + am/is/are + past participle (V3) (+ by agent)
blueprintItems.example: Newspapers are printed every morning by the local press.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Past Simple Passive Formula
blueprintItems.formula: Object + was/were + past participle (V3) (+ by agent)
blueprintItems.example: The historic building was damaged by the severe storm last night.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: News Report Structure
blueprintItems.formula: Headline + Lead Sentence (Active/Passive) + Supporting Details (Passive Voice)
blueprintItems.example: Local Museum Robbed. Valuable paintings were stolen from the downtown gallery on Tuesday.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always match the auxiliary verb (am, is, are, was, were) with the new subject in passive sentences.
mechanicsRules.badExample: The windows was broken during the match.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: The windows were broken during the match.
mechanicsRules.why: Windows is plural, so it requires 'were' instead of 'was'.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use past participle forms correctly for regular and irregular verbs in passive sentences.
mechanicsRules.badExample: A new bridge is build across the river.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: A new bridge is built across the river.
mechanicsRules.why: The past participle of 'build' is 'built', not 'build'.

mechanicsRules.rule: Capitalize the first letter of every sentence and all proper nouns in news headlines.
mechanicsRules.badExample: new bridge opened in london by the mayor.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: New bridge opened in London by the mayor.
mechanicsRules.why: Proper nouns like London and the start of every sentence must be capitalized.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Making the News and Passive Voice

content.summary: This speaking module focuses on reporting news stories and using the passive voice correctly in spoken English. Clear articulation of past participles and appropriate sentence stress help listeners understand who or what received the action.
content.audioGuidance: When speaking the passive voice, emphasize the main verb and the agent if it is introduced with the word by. Pause briefly after reporting verbs to make your speech sound natural and engaging.

pillars.name: Passive Verb Clarity
pillars.target: Pronounce auxiliary verbs and past participles distinctly
pillars.explanation: Do not swallow the auxiliary verb was or were. Ensure the ending of the past participle like invented or reported is clearly heard.

pillars.name: Sentence Stress in News Reports
pillars.target: Stress key nouns and main verbs
pillars.explanation: In news broadcasts, focus words carry the primary information. Words like journalist, crop, and admitted must stand out against grammar words.

pillars.name: Reporting Intonation
pillars.target: Use falling intonation for completed factual reports
pillars.explanation: When stating a news fact in the passive voice, drop your pitch at the end of the clause to signal certainty and completion.

pillars.name: Pacing and Pausing
pillars.target: Group words into meaningful thought units
pillars.explanation: Pause between the subject and the passive verb phrase to give your listener time to process the information.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: Notice that the main stress shifts to the second syllable in both forms, but the past tense adds an extra syllable at the end.
The stress remains on the second syllable when changing from the verb to the noun.

The main stress stays on the second syllable while adding the past tense ending.
